I know for certain it's not biologically a luna moth. Luna moth's are always characterized by their pale green to yellow green wings and white bodies, however even among Saturniidae this sculpture lacks proper features.

The wings and eye spots are correctly shaped to be some form of Saturniidae, but the sculpture falls apart anatomically in the thorax and the head. The thorax of a propper Saturniidae is wide to the point of being close to round and covered in a light hair. The head is very small relative to it's body, and it's mouth parts are near non-existant. Most Saturniidae do not eat after pupating, surviving only long enough to mate, lay eggs and die. Because of this, if you look head on at a saturniidae it looks anatomically like it has "thick shoulders" and a tiny head.

https://c1.staticflickr.com/9/8077/8435321378_b893bf998e_b.jpg https://i.ytimg.com/vi/Mk_TnAi8CY8/maxresdefault.jpg https://www.google.com/search?q=Saturniidae&source=lnms&tbm=isch&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwj87NTVs-jJAhUCXD4KHf9ICFoQ_AUIBygB&biw=1366&bih=631#imgrc=mDsGftviVq4SCM%3A

Finally, the antennae are completely wrong. Saturniidae do not have pronounced stalks, like most moths their antennae are feathery and close to their head. The antennae shape of this sculpture does not fit any moth of the genus of which the luna moth is a part.

However, I am not an entomologist, I just have these things near where I live, and this was a good excuse to learn a bit about them on a relaxing saturday morning.

EDIT: for contrast, here is the warmer climate variety of luna, giving you the full range of this moth's appearance: http://www.birdsandblooms.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/Luna-Moth-Body.jpg

there other moth's called "moon moths" in saturniidae, but they are separate from true luna moths, and even they look nothing like this sculpture.
